title: Orchestrate dedicated pools for geotolerant throughput and residency enforcement
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Goal: implement an orchestration policy and runtime hooks that let us offer explicit throughput guarantees on Dedicated capacity across regional and multi-zone deployments while enforcing data residency constraints.

Scope:
- Define a placement and routing contract for "geotolerant" dedicated pools (ability to serve primarily from in-residency zones with controlled cross-zone overflow).
- Autoscaling policy primitives: warm-reserve lanes, headroom-based scale-up, staggered drain for scale-down, and quota-backed emergency burst.
- Throughput guarantees: token-sliced reservation model (client-visible min RPS/TPU-equivalent tokens) and internal admission control that respects both locality and reserved capacity.
- Residency enforcement: tag-based data residency, KMS key scoping per residency region, audit hooks for cross-zone data egress, and opt-in cross-zone fallback with explicit logging and customer notification.

Non-goals: global active-active state sync for customer KV caches (we'll rely on per-region caches + invalidation), reworking lower-level kernel selection (separate runtime optimization work).

Success metrics:
- Demonstrate 99th percentile per-customer latency within SLA under 90% reserved utilization in-region.
- Controlled cross-zone overflow ratio < 3% in steady state for customers with residency constraints (configurable).
- Autoscaling time-to-add-capacity under typical burst: < 60s for warm-reserve path, < 180s for new instance path.

Engineering considerations and trade-offs:
1) Soft-affinity vs hard pinning: hard pinning simplifies residency enforcement but reduces utilization and increases cost. We propose soft-affinity with prioritized routing and an allowlist for strict-residency customers.
2) Warm-reserve cost: keeping standby GPUs per region increases unit cost. We'll expose a tunable "warm-reserve" parameter to customers and provide recommended defaults based on workload profile.
3) Admission control placement decision point: place logic at edge proxy vs central orchestrator. Edge decision reduces control plane latency but complicates global orchestration; we will implement a hybrid: primary decision at orchestrator + fast edge re-routing for emergency fallback.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- M1 (Design): finalize policy model, residency tags, and admission control API (Confluence design doc link in attachments). Target: 2025-11-14.
- M2 (Runtime): implement admission control primitives, warm-reserve lane support, token-sliced reservation accounting. Target: 2025-12-12.
- M3 (Orchestrator): integrate with fleet manager for prioritized placement and coordinated scale-up/scale-down. Target: 2026-01-05.
- M4 (Customer controls + Console): Console UI for residency settings and throughput reservations, alerting on cross-zone overflow. Target: 2026-01-20.

Links / artifacts:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood/company/dedicated-geotolerant-orchestration
- Architecture sketch (Drive): https://drive.redwood/company/drive/d/1xOrchSketch
- Benchmark notebook: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pulls/274
- Prototype PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4123 (admission control), https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/99 (placement policy)

Open questions:
- Default warm-reserve sizing heuristic for mixed workloads (LLM streaming vs batch embed): proposal to use 20th percentile peak CPU/GPU footprint over last 24h.
- How to surface residency-compliance events to customers without leaking internal topology (recommend structured event with residency-flag + anonymized location).

Rollout strategy: beta with a small set of existing Dedicated customers (3 customers across NA & EU) for early validation. Gradual ramp with observability hooks for cross-zone overflow and cost telemetry.
